justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift across horizons, starting near 145.2 for the one-day forecast and gradually rising to 148.0 at one month. The one-day estimate is anchored heavily by recent price action and momentum — assuming no major overnight catalysts, prices tend to mean-revert or continue short-term trends, so I placed the estimate close to the last observed level with only a slight upward bias. At the one-week horizon, I incorporated a small drift premium reflecting the general tendency of the underlying asset to trend modestly higher in the current macro environment. By one month, the estimate reflects a continuation of that drift compounded over more trading sessions, though the incremental move remains conservative given the absence of a strong fundamental catalyst to justify a sharper directional call.

The confidence interval widths expand substantially as the horizon lengthens, which reflects the compounding of daily volatility over time. At one day, the 90% interval spans roughly 7.4 points, consistent with typical daily realized volatility for this type of asset. By one week, the interval widens to 16 points, and at one month it reaches 32 points — roughly proportional to the square-root-of-time scaling one would expect from a random walk assumption layered on top of the directional drift. I also widened the intervals slightly more than pure volatility math would suggest, because uncertainty about the macro backdrop, central bank communications, and liquidity conditions adds fat-tail risk that simple historical volatility may understate.

There are several specific risks that could push outcomes well outside these stated intervals. On the upside, a surprise dovish pivot from a major central bank, a significantly better-than-expected economic data release, or a resolution of a geopolitical tension could trigger a sharp rally beyond 164 at the monthly horizon. On the downside, a renewed inflation shock, an unexpected credit event in a systemically important institution, or an escalation of geopolitical conflict could drive prices below 132 or even lower. Liquidity events — such as forced de-leveraging by large institutional players or a sudden spike in volatility indices — represent a particular tail risk because they can produce price moves that dwarf normal distributional assumptions and invalidate even wide confidence intervals constructed from historical data.
